    Week 5 · Live session

    When lines are not enough¶

    Altamar's straight lines explain part of its rates and its cancellations, but the hotels' seasons and the risky bookings made three months ahead do not follow a line. Today you will fit models that bend, see how they can fool themselves, and tune them with cross-validation so they don't.

    • 4 hours
    • 8 ideas
    • Runs in your browser
    • Case: a nonlinear model

    Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the clean bookings, makes the same train/test splits as weeks 3 and 4 (25% test, random_state=42), and defines small helpers that print comparison tables and turn a tree into readable rules.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    # Setup: libraries, the clean Altamar data, the train/test splits and a few helpers.
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, KFold, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error, roc_auc_score, accuracy_score
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv")
df["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month

CATS = ["hotel", "room_type", "customer_type", "channel", "deposit", "country"]
NUMS = ["lead_time_days", "nights", "weekend_nights", "adults", "children", "repeat_guest",
        "previous_cancellations", "special_requests", "parking", "arrival_month"]

def rate_X(rows, month_as="number", drop_first=False):
    """Inputs for the rate question. The linear model gets one column per month (session 3);
    a tree can use the month as a number and group the months itself."""
    X = rows[NUMS + CATS].copy()
    cats = CATS + (["arrival_month"] if month_as == "dummies" else [])
    if month_as == "dummies":
        X["arrival_month"] = X["arrival_month"].astype(str)
    X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=cats, drop_first=drop_first, dtype=float)
    return X if drop_first else X.reindex(columns=RATE_COLS[month_as], fill_value=0.0)

RATE_COLS = {m: list(rate_X(df, m, drop_first=True).columns) for m in ["number", "dummies"]}
Xr, Xr_lin, y_rate = rate_X(df, "number"), rate_X(df, "dummies"), df["adr"]
Xr_train, Xr_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(Xr, y_rate, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
Xl_train, Xl_test = train_test_split(Xr_lin, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)  # the same bookings

Xc = pd.get_dummies(df[NUMS + CATS + ["adr"]], columns=CATS, drop_first=True, dtype=float)
y_cancel = df["canceled"]
Xc_train, Xc_test, yc_train, yc_test = train_test_split(Xc, y_cancel, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_cancel)

def rate_scores(name, model, X_train, X_test):
    """One row of a comparison table for the rate question."""
    return {"model": name, "R² train": r2_score(yr_train, model.predict(X_train)),
            "R² test": r2_score(yr_test, model.predict(X_test)),
            "typical error, test (USD)": mean_absolute_error(yr_test, model.predict(X_test))}

def cancel_scores(name, model, X_train, X_test):
    """One row of a comparison table for the cancellation question."""
    return {"model": name, "accuracy train": accuracy_score(yc_train, model.predict(X_train)),
            "accuracy test": accuracy_score(yc_test, model.predict(X_test)),
            "AUC test": roc_auc_score(yc_test, model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])}

def table(rows):
    """Print a list of score rows as a small, rounded table."""
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").round(3).to_string(), "\n")

def tree_rules(model, columns):
    """Every leaf of a fitted tree as a readable rule, with its size and its answer."""
    t, rows = model.tree_, []
    def walk(node, conds):
        if t.children_left[node] == -1:
            v = t.value[node][0]
            answer = v[1] / v.sum() if len(v) > 1 else v[0]
            rows.append({"rule": " and ".join(describe(conds)) or "all bookings",
                         "bookings": int(t.n_node_samples[node]), "answer": answer})
            return
        f, thr = columns[t.feature[node]], t.threshold[node]
        walk(t.children_left[node], conds + [(f, "<=", thr)])
        walk(t.children_right[node], conds + [(f, ">", thr)])
    walk(0, [])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

LEAD_BINS = [0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 200, 400]
LEAD_LABELS = ["0–15", "16–30", "31–45", "46–60", "61–90", "91–120", "121–150", "151–200", "201+"]
MONTHS = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]

def describe(conds):
    """Merge the conditions on a path into short, plain phrases."""
    lo, hi, out, is_, not_ = {}, {}, [], {}, {}
    for f, op, thr in conds:
        cat = next((c for c in CATS if f.startswith(c + "_")), None)
        if cat:
            (not_ if op == "<=" else is_).setdefault(cat, []).append(f[len(cat) + 1:])
        elif op == "<=":
            hi[f] = min(hi.get(f, np.inf), thr)
        else:
            lo[f] = max(lo.get(f, -np.inf), thr)
    for cat in dict.fromkeys(c for c in CATS if c in is_ or c in not_):
        name = cat.replace("_", " ")
        out.append(f"{name} is {is_[cat][0]}" if cat in is_ else f"{name} is not {not_[cat][0]}" if len(not_[cat]) == 1 else f"{name} is neither {' nor '.join(not_[cat])}")
    for f in dict.fromkeys(f for f, _, _ in conds if f in lo or f in hi):
        if f == "adr":
            a, b = lo.get(f), hi.get(f)
            out.append(f"rate USD {a:.0f}–{b:.0f}" if a and b else f"rate > USD {a:.0f}" if a else f"rate ≤ USD {b:.0f}")
            continue
        a = int(np.floor(lo[f])) + 1 if f in lo else None
        b = int(np.floor(hi[f])) if f in hi else None
        if f == "arrival_month":
            a, b = a or 1, b or 12
            out.append(f"arrives in {MONTHS[a - 1]}" + (f"–{MONTHS[b - 1]}" if b > a else ""))
            continue
        name = f.replace("_", " ").replace(" days", "")
        out.append(f"{name} {a}–{b}" if a is not None and b is not None else f"{name} ≥ {a}" if a is not None else f"{name} = 0" if b == 0 else f"{name} ≤ {b}")
    return out

print(f"{len(df):,} bookings. Rate question: {len(Xr_train):,} train / {len(Xr_test):,} test. "
      f"Cancellation question: {len(Xc_train):,} train / {len(Xc_test):,} test ({y_cancel.mean():.1%} cancel).")

    5,964 bookings. Rate question: 4,473 train / 1,491 test. Cancellation question: 4,473 train / 1,491 test (33.7% cancel).

    01 Previously at Altamar¶

    In weeks 3 and 4 the management team got two straight-line models:

    • Rates: a linear regression with one column per month explained about 74% of the variation in nightly rates (R² ≈ 0.74), with a typical error of about USD 20.
    • Cancellations: a logistic regression ranked risky bookings with an AUC ≈ 0.74.

    Both are useful, and both left money on the table. This cell refits them so we have a baseline to beat.

table([cancel_scores("logistic regression", logit, Xc_train, Xc_test)])

    Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas peak in the summer (January–February, and December), Puerto Varas again in the July winter holidays, while Santiago dips in summer and rises with the September–November conferences. The linear model gives each month one bonus that is the same for all three hotels, so it cannot draw three different seasons.

    Now cancellations. This chart shows the share of bookings that cancel, by how far ahead they were made.

    Risk climbs from about 16% for last-minute bookings to about 70% for bookings made 61 to 120 days ahead, then falls back to about 40%. A logistic regression can only say "the further ahead, the riskier" (or the opposite): one direction, all the way.

    Business takeaway: both questions have shapes that bend: a peak, a dip, a hump. Today's models are built to bend.

    02 Curves: a line that bends¶

    The simplest way to bend a line is to add powers of the input: day, day², day³… A degree-2 polynomial is a U; each extra degree allows one more bend.

    The simulator uses 100 Standard-room bookings at Viña del Mar. Raise the degree slowly. Then press Draw other bookings at degree 12 to 15 and watch the ends of the year.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

    This cell fits three curves to Viña del Mar's Standard-room rates by arrival date: a straight line, a U (degree 2) and the degree you choose. The faint band on each side is outside the year: watch what the curves do there. ✏️ Try DEGREE = 3, 8 and 15.

    # ✏️ Change these settings
HOTEL = "Viña del Mar"
DEGREE = 12
h = df[(df["hotel"] == HOTEL) & (df["room_type"] == "Standard")]
day = pd.to_datetime(h["arrival_date"]).dt.dayofyear / 365 * 12          # 0 = 1 Jan, 12 = 31 Dec
d_tr, d_te, r_tr, r_te = train_test_split(day, h["adr"], test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
grid = np.linspace(-0.6, 12.6, 300)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
plt.scatter(d_tr, r_tr, s=8, alpha=0.25, color="gray", label="bookings (train)")
for deg in [1, 2, DEGREE]:
    curve = np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit(d_tr, r_tr, deg)
    plt.plot(grid, curve(grid), lw=2, label=f"degree {deg}: typical test error USD {mean_absolute_error(r_te, curve(d_te)):.1f}")
plt.axvspan(-0.6, 0, color="gray", alpha=0.12); plt.axvspan(12, 12.6, color="gray", alpha=0.12)
plt.ylim(0, 300); plt.legend(); plt.title(f"{HOTEL}: polynomial curves for the season")
plt.xlabel("arrival date (months into the year)"); plt.ylabel("nightly rate (USD)")
plt.show()

    The U already beats the line clearly: the line has to slope one way through the year and misses the summer at one end. Higher degrees gain little on new bookings and become fragile at the edges: just outside the data, on the shaded bands, they swing wildly, so a booking on 31 December or 1 January can get an absurd rate.

    Watch out: a curve is chosen input by input and hotel by hotel. Altamar has a dozen inputs and three hotels with different seasons: hand-crafting curves and their combinations does not scale. We need a model that finds the bends by itself.

    03 A tree asks questions¶

    A decision tree does not draw a curve. It asks yes/no questions: does the guest arrive in January or February? Is it a suite? Each answer sends the booking down a branch, and at the end of the branch the prediction is simply the average rate of the training bookings that ended up there.

    So a tree answers with averages of groups of similar bookings. Along one input its answer is a staircase. Add depth in the simulator and watch the groups split.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

    Now the real thing: a regression tree on all the inputs, compared with last week's line on the same test bookings. max_depth is the number of questions a booking answers at most. ✏️ Try MAX_DEPTH = 3, 6 and 10.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    # ✏️ Change these settings
MAX_DEPTH = 6
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train)
table([rate_scores("linear regression (month dummies)", lin, Xl_train, Xl_test),
       rate_scores(f"tree, max_depth={MAX_DEPTH}", tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)])
print(f"The tree sorts the {len(Xr_train):,} training bookings into {tree.get_n_leaves()} groups.")
    # ✏️ Change these settings MAX_DEPTH = 6 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) table([rate_scores("linear regression (month dummies)", lin, Xl_train, Xl_test), rate_scores(f"tree, max_depth={MAX_DEPTH}", tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) print(f"The tree sorts the {len(Xr_train):,} training bookings into {tree.get_n_leaves()} groups.")
                                       R² train  R² test  typical error, test (USD)
model                                                                          
linear regression (month dummies)     0.740    0.738                     20.483
tree, max_depth=6                     0.857    0.845                     16.740 

The tree sorts the 4,473 training bookings into 62 groups.

    With MAX_DEPTH = 6 the tree explains about 85% of the variation (R² ≈ 0.85 against 0.74) and its typical error falls from about USD 20 to about USD 17 a night, about 15% of the average rate. It found the seasons of each hotel by itself: nobody told it that January means something different in Santiago and in Viña del Mar.

    To read a tree, keep it small. This cell draws a depth-3 tree for the rate.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    small = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train)
plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))
plot_tree(small, feature_names=list(Xr_train.columns), filled=True, impurity=False, precision=0, fontsize=9)
plt.title("A depth-3 tree for the nightly rate: each box shows the question, the bookings and their average rate")
plt.show()
    small = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6)) plot_tree(small, feature_names=list(Xr_train.columns), filled=True, impurity=False, precision=0, fontsize=9) plt.title("A depth-3 tree for the nightly rate: each box shows the question, the bookings and their average rate") plt.show()

    Read it top-down, like a pricing manual. Each box asks a question (left branch = yes, right = no), and value is the average rate of the bookings that reached it. The first question is the season: does the guest arrive in January or February? In summer the next question is the hotel (Santiago or not), the rest of the year it is the room. The bottom boxes are eight business rules, each an average rate for a group of similar bookings.

    This cell prints the same eight rules as plain sentences, from the most to the least expensive.

    04 How a tree chooses a question¶

    At every step the tree tries every input and every cut point, and keeps the question that leaves the two groups least mixed.

    • For cancellations, "mixed" means a group with cancelled and kept bookings together. It is measured with the Gini impurity: 0 for a pure group, 0.5 for a 50/50 mix.
    • For rates, "mixed" means rates that are far from their group's average. The tree keeps the question that most reduces that error, which is what you watched in the staircase.

    Try it with twenty bookings: drag the line, then let the tree try every split.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

    For the curious: Gini of a group = 1 − (share cancelled)² − (share kept)². A question is scored by the Gini of its two sides, weighted by their size; the lowest score wins. For regression the score is the squared error around each side's average.

    The tree then repeats the same search inside each side, and again, level after level. The next simulator grows a cancellation tree on two inputs, lead time and rate. Look at what the tree does with risk that rises and then falls.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

    Now on Altamar's full data. This cell fits a depth-3 classification tree for cancellations and prints its eight groups, from the riskiest to the safest. answer is the share of training bookings in that group that cancelled.

    The first question is lead time ≤ 45 days, the same cut the twenty bookings suggested. The riskiest group is bookings made 46 to 132 days ahead through an online travel agency (about 3 in 4 cancel): the three-months-out peak, found without anyone telling the tree. The safest are bookings made up to 45 days ahead by guests with no previous cancellations, at up to about USD 138 (12%). And for far-ahead bookings outside the agencies, a non-refundable deposit halves the risk (51% → 24%).

    Business takeaway: each rule is a segment the operations team can act on: a reminder, a deposit policy, how many rooms to oversell.

    ☕ Break. Ten minutes. When we come back: what happens if we let the tree keep asking questions forever?

    05 When trees memorize¶

    Every extra level lets the tree carve smaller groups. With no limit it keeps going until every group is pure: often a single booking. It then knows the training bookings by heart, noise included, and that knowledge does not travel to new bookings.

    Turn the dial from 1 to 15 and watch the two errors on the right. Then switch to cross-validation.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

model

Groups: 4,465 for the rate tree, 956 for the cancellation tree.
Accuracy of saying 'nobody cancels': 66.3%

    The cancellation tree is 100% right on the bookings it learned from and about 66% right on new ones: no better than saying "nobody cancels". Its AUC drops to about 0.62, worse than the logistic regression. It memorized 4,473 bookings in almost a thousand tiny groups.

    The rate tree also gets a perfect training score (R² = 1.00) but about 0.88 on the test: a gap of 0.12. Rates follow strong rules, so memorizing hurts less, but the gap says the same thing: a training score is not evidence. The question is how deep to go.

    06 Cross-validation and tuning¶

    To pick the depth we must compare depths on bookings the tree did not learn from. But if we use the test set to choose, it is no longer an honest final check, and one test is just one opinion: a different split could favour a different depth.

    Cross-validation solves both problems: it cuts the training bookings into 5 folds, lets each fold be the validation set once, and averages the 5 scores. The test set stays locked until the very end. The scores in this simulator are real Altamar results.

    ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

    This cell runs 5-fold cross-validation for six depths of the rate tree (30 fits, a few seconds) and plots the average validation R² with its spread across folds.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    DEPTHS = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
rows = []
for d in DEPTHS:
    s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xr_train, yr_train, cv=cv, scoring="r2")
    rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()})
rate_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
plt.errorbar(rate_cv["depth"], rate_cv["mean"], yerr=rate_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4)
plt.title("Rate tree: 5-fold cross-validated R² by depth")
plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation R²")
plt.show()
best_rate_depth = int(rate_cv.loc[rate_cv["mean"].idxmax(), "depth"])
print(f"Best depth for the rate: {best_rate_depth} (average R² {rate_cv['mean'].max():.3f})")
    DEPTHS = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12] cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS: s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xr_train, yr_train, cv=cv, scoring="r2") rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()}) rate_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.errorbar(rate_cv["depth"], rate_cv["mean"], yerr=rate_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4) plt.title("Rate tree: 5-fold cross-validated R² by depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation R²") plt.show() best_rate_depth = int(rate_cv.loc[rate_cv["mean"].idxmax(), "depth"]) print(f"Best depth for the rate: {best_rate_depth} (average R² {rate_cv['mean'].max():.3f})")
    Best depth for the rate: 10 (average R² 0.866)

    For the rate, R² rises fast up to depth 8 and then flattens: depth 10 is the best average, with depth 8 practically tied. Rates follow many real rules (hotel × season × room × channel), so the tree can use many questions before it starts memorizing.

    The same search for cancellations, scored with AUC, the metric of week 4:

for d in DEPTHS:

    rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()})
cancel_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
plt.errorbar(cancel_cv["depth"], cancel_cv["mean"], yerr=cancel_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4, color="#c85a24")

    cv5 = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS: s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xc_train, yc_train, cv=cv5, scoring="roc_auc") rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()}) cancel_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.errorbar(cancel_cv["depth"], cancel_cv["mean"], yerr=cancel_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4, color="#c85a24") plt.title("Cancellation tree: 5-fold cross-validated AUC by depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation AUC") plt.show() best_cancel_depth = int(cancel_cv.loc[cancel_cv["mean"].idxmax(), "depth"]) print(f"Best depth for cancellations: {best_cancel_depth} (average AUC {cancel_cv['mean'].max():.3f})")
    Best depth for cancellations: 4 (average AUC 0.780)

    Cancellations show the full U-shape: AUC peaks at depth 4 and falls steadily after it, because whether a guest cancels is far noisier than the rate. Different questions, different best depths: that is why we tune.

    Only now do we touch the test set, once, with the chosen depths retrained on all the training bookings.

    The test scores land close to the cross-validated ones (rate R² ≈ 0.89, cancellation AUC ≈ 0.75): cross-validation told the truth about bookings it had not seen. That is the point of the method: you can trust the number before you deploy.

    Where does the cancellation tree win? This chart compares, for each lead-time band of the test bookings, the share that really cancelled with the average risk each model predicted.

    test = df.loc[Xc_test.index]
lead_band = pd.cut(test["lead_time_days"], LEAD_BINS, labels=LEAD_LABELS, include_lowest=True)
view = pd.DataFrame({"actual": yc_test, "logistic": logit.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1],
                     "tree": cancel_tree.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1]}).groupby(lead_band, observed=True).mean()

    Where the tree is better: it follows the hump (low risk last-minute, a peak two to four months out, lower again far ahead), while the logistic line keeps climbing and misses the peak. On rates it follows each hotel's own seasons and cuts the typical error by a third (USD 20 → 13).

    What it costs:

    • Step-shaped answers: two bookings one day apart can get rates a full step apart.
    • Less stable: a slightly different sample can change the first question and the rules.
    • No extrapolation: beyond what it has seen, it repeats the last group's average.

    Next week: many trees voting together keep the strengths and soften these costs.

    08 Case clinic: a nonlinear model¶

    This week's step for your team (see the applied case): a decision tree, its depth chosen with cross-validation.

    1. Open the case toolkit with your data and settings from weeks 1–4.
    2. Run section 08 Decision tree with cross-validation (it tries depths 2 to 10 with 5 folds).
    3. Record the chosen depth, its cross-validated score (± spread) and its test score, next to your linear model from week 3.
    4. Print the tree's top rules and write two sentences: which rule surprises you, and what a manager would do with it.
    5. If the training score is far above the cross-validated score, say so: that is overfitting, and it belongs in your limitations.

    Next: the lab lets you tune the tree yourself (depth, minimum group size, cross-validation) and ends with this week's graded quiz. Week 6 grows forests and boosting.
